clue.text: Church at rear of Newcastle United's ground

parts.note: ch is the short form printed on maps beside a church

indicators.note: The rear of anything is its back end, so only the final letter of the word named next is taken.

parts.note: the letter at the back of Newcastle
a couple united in marriage are wed

explanation.surface: The church standing behind the stadium where Newcastle United play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newcastle United' begs to be read as one thing, the football club whose ground the surface points at, and the setter splits the name in half. Only the last letter of the first half survives.
explanation.definitionFit: Chewed food has been ground between the teeth, and 'ground' is the past tense of grind, matching the tense of the answer.

clue.text: In truth, a Hampshire country estate feature

indicators.note: 'In' says the letters are sitting inside the words that follow, unbroken and in the order given.

parts.note: the four letters run on from the tail of the first word into the head of the last, across both the comma and the word break

explanation.surface: An assurance about something you would find on a Hampshire estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In truth' reads as an aside promising honesty, which is exactly why the eye skims it. The name is said to come from the cry of surprise let out by anyone who nearly walks into one.
explanation.definitionFit: A ha-ha is the sunken ditch-and-wall fence at the edge of an English country-house lawn, keeping livestock off the garden without a hedge to spoil the view.

clue.text: Disheartened Brummie enters spouting 'Good health!'

indicators.note: A disheartened word has had its heart torn out, leaving only what stood at either end.
Whatever enters a place ends up inside it, so these letters land within the other chunk rather than beside it.

parts.note: water welling up from the ground is water spouting, and the word opens after its fourth letter
Brummie stripped of everything between its first and last letter

explanation.surface: A man from Birmingham bursting in mid-flow with a toast.
explanation.walkthrough: Brummie is the setter's own pseudonym as well as a native of Birmingham, and here it is only a word to gut. 'Spouting' looks like the talking the Brummie is doing and means a spring of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellbeing is the state of being well — good health widened out to cover a person's whole condition, body and mind.

clue.text: Force gets you finally in gear

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word just given, so only its last letter is taken.
'In' puts the letter just found inside the word that follows rather than in front of it.

parts.note: gear is clothing, and the word opens after its first letter
the last letter of you

explanation.surface: Pressure that finally gets somebody into their kit.
explanation.walkthrough: On the surface 'in gear' is the idiom about getting moving, and the wordplay needs gear in its older sense of clothing. 'You' is not the solver being addressed, just a word with a last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is force applied to make somebody act — a confession under duress is one squeezed out by threat.

clue.text: City fans unruly but free from sin?

indicators.note: An unruly crowd will not keep its lines, and letters described that way will not keep their order either.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Supporters of a football club behaving badly at the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C sends you hunting for a particular club when the word is only there to be stirred. The question mark admits the definition is a whole phrase rather than a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanctify is to make holy, and making someone holy is precisely freeing them from sin.

clue.text: Classic film debut of Sesame Street not established internally

indicators.note: A debut is a first appearance, so what is wanted is the letter the word makes its entrance with.
Internally means in the middle rather than at either end, so this chunk drops in between the two pieces around it.

parts.note: the opening letter of Sesame, taken on its own
something not yet set — jelly, concrete, a date in the diary — is unset
a boulevard is a broad street lined with trees

explanation.surface: A famous film making its first appearance on Sesame Street, where nothing has been settled indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sesame Street' is one title in the reader's head, so splitting it is the whole difficulty: only Sesame is used, and the other half is the word for street. Norma Desmond's line about being big while the pictures got small comes from this film.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunset Boulevard is Billy Wilder's 1950 picture about a forgotten silent star, long since fixed in the canon of classics.

clue.text: Meant to change some lines for worm

indicators.note: A thing told to change does not come back as it went in, and letters change by swapping places.

parts.note: the five letters rearranged
an ode is a poem, which is some lines of verse

explanation.surface: An actor who intended to rewrite a few of his lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meant to change' reads as an intention never carried out, which is how the instruction hides in plain sight. ODE is the crossword's standard answer whenever lines are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A nematode is a roundworm, so 'worm' is the everyday name for the creature the answer gives the scientific one for.

clue.text: Tight garment cut in circles

indicators.note: Something that circles keeps going round, and letters sent round like that come back in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A clinging garment cut on the round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like tailoring and is fodder instead, which leaves the entire wordplay in two short words the eye runs straight past. Five letters from five letters, with nothing else in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic is the close-fitting jacket of a soldier's or police officer's uniform, so 'tight' describes the cut and 'garment' the thing itself.

clue.text: It can douse the flames of passion — e.g. with nine shakes

parts.note: fire is passion itself — a speech delivered with fire

indicators.note: A thing that shakes has its parts thrown out of place, and letters shaken settle in a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder: the abbreviation without its stops, plus the number written out

explanation.surface: Whatever it is that kills a romance, nine good shakes of it will do the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash lets the second half pass as an example of the first when it is a set of instructions. 'Flames of passion' is one phrase on the surface and is torn in two by the parsing.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire engine is the truck that turns out to put a blaze out, so the definition names it by the job it exists to do.

clue.text: South American country seizes medic and, briefly, kids

indicators.note: To seize something is to grab hold of it, and what is grabbed ends up held inside.
Said briefly, a word shrinks to the shortest form people actually pronounce.

parts.note: Chile is the long strip down the Pacific coast, and it opens after its fourth letter
dr is the doctor's title in front of a name
and spoken in a hurry is 'n', as in rock 'n' roll

explanation.surface: A Latin American state arresting a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' at the end looks like a verb — the country is joking — and it is the plural noun being defined. The commas around 'briefly' let a piece of wordplay pass as an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Kids is the informal word every parent uses for their children, and both are plural nouns for the young of the family.

clue.text: Crew on capsized craft chant

indicators.note: A capsized boat has turned right over, so the word it applies to is written backwards.

parts.note: to man a boat is to crew it
craft is art, turned round

explanation.surface: The crew clinging to an upturned boat and chanting.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is nautical, which is what makes 'craft' look like the boat when it means skill. Crossword setters use craft for art so often it is worth filing away.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantra is a formula chanted over and over in meditation, so 'chant' names it by the only thing it is ever used for.

clue.text: Like the Two Ronnies' big show in base

indicators.note: 'In' drops what has just been clued inside the word that follows.

parts.note: the bed of a machine or a road is the base it rests on, and it splits after its second letter
a spectacle is a show staged on a grand scale

explanation.surface: The Two Ronnies putting on a lavish revue at a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' invites the army camp the surface wants and means the foundation something rests on. Ronnie Barker and Ronnie Corbett fronted BBC sketch comedy for two decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Ronnies wore heavy dark spectacles on screen, so being like them is being bespectacled — a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Nebulous picture of cold, obtrusive, southern promontory

parts.note: c is the cold tap and the cold wash
a loud tie is an obtrusive one
s is the compass point on any map
a cape is the headland that juts into the sea

explanation.surface: A hazy painting of a bleak, overbearing headland down south.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make a list of adjectives, which is why four separate instructions read as one description of a coast. 'Nebulous' belongs to the definition and does the misleading anyway, meaning vague on the surface and cloudy in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloudscape is a picture whose subject is the sky, and nebulous is the adjective for cloud, so the definition says cloud-picture twice over.

clue.text: Southern French town omits one from legal defence

indicators.note: omits means leaves out, so a letter is taken out of the defence

parts.note: an alibi is a defence that the accused was elsewhere
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A French town in the south drops someone from its legal defence team.
explanation.walkthrough: ALIBI has two I's; dropping either leaves the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Albi is a cathedral town in the Tarn department of southern France, birthplace of Toulouse-Lautrec.

clue.text: Wicked, popular, mature repartee

parts.note: wicked and bad are the same charge
what is in this season is what is popular
to mature is to age, as cheese and whisky do

explanation.surface: Three verdicts in a row on somebody's banter.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjectives run on so smoothly that the sentence reads as praise for a person's talk rather than as three separate words to write down. 'Mature' is the verb to age, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Badinage is light teasing talk, which is repartee in its everyday sense — quick exchanges made for amusement rather than for winning.

clue.text: Teddy possibly exploding with anger

definitions.note: A teddy is one garment where nightwear is the uncountable class it belongs to, and 'possibly' is the setter's flag that the definition offers an example.

indicators.note: Something exploding throws its parts everywhere, and the letters come down in a new arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A teddy bear blowing up in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: The teddy is a bear on the surface and a woman's one-piece in the answer, which is what 'possibly' is there to license. 'With' belongs to the fodder rather than joining the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A teddy is a one-piece camisole and knickers worn in bed, which makes it one item of nightwear.

clue.text: Thousands of pounds prior to working — it's all relative

definitions.note: The answer is a person and the definition is a catchphrase; 'relative' is the word doing the work, dressed up as the saying about everything depending on how you look at it.

indicators.note: Prior to means before, so the letters just clued are written in front of the ones that follow.

parts.note: a grand is a thousand pounds in British slang, and several of them are grands
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Serious money demanded up front, and a shrug about how serious it really is.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash lets the definition pass as a wry comment on the sum of money, which is the hardest place in a clue to spot one. 'Working' is the switched-on machine rather than the labour.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandson is a relative, and the idiom is bent so its last word means a member of the family rather than a matter of comparison.

clue.text: Peak month for initially tucking into ragu perhaps

indicators.note: Initially asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing more of it.
Perhaps offers the word as a possibility rather than a fixed thing, which licenses any arrangement of its letters.

parts.note: jun is June as the calendar prints it

indicators.note: To tuck into something is to get right inside it, so the letter goes within the other word rather than beside it.

parts.note: the four letters of the sauce rearranged, then opened after the first
the letter for begins with

explanation.surface: The best month of the year for getting stuck into a plate of ragu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is an unusual anagram indicator, and it catches solvers because in most clues it flags a definition by example instead. 'Peak month' reads as one phrase and only the first word of it defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jungfrau is a mountain in the Bernese Alps above Interlaken, so 'peak' names the answer by its bare category.

clue.text: Working to dispose of international medal

indicators.note: dispose of means get rid of, so the letter is removed

parts.note: going means working, as in 'the machine is going'

explanation.surface: Someone works hard to get rid of an international award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' is GOING, as a clock is going; drop the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Gong is informal British slang for a medal or award, especially an honour like a knighthood.

clue.text: Fairy king goes in through part of tower

indicators.note: What goes in is placed inside, so the letters just clued sit within the word that follows.

parts.note: to travel by a place is to travel through it, and the two letters open up to take the rest
an elf is the fairy of three letters
r is rex, Latin for king, the letter monarchs sign after their name

explanation.surface: A fairy king making his way in through the tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairy king' reads as one person, Oberon in the wood, and splits into two separate pieces. 'Through' is the preposition the picture needs and a two-letter word in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The belfry is the stage of a tower where the bells hang, so it is one part of the structure rather than the whole of it.

clue.text: Fancy teen's garment split

indicators.note: Fancy work is elaborate rather than plain, and letters given the fancy treatment do not stay in their plain order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters once the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: An ornate outfit for a teenager, slit down one side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' comes last and reads as one more detail of the garment, which is where the definition hides. The apostrophe counts for nothing when the letters are gathered up.
explanation.definitionFit: An estrangement is a split between people who were once close — a split in a family, a couple's split — the noun for the breach itself.

clue.text: Become entangled with party on left

indicators.note: In a down clue, whatever sits on something else is written above it, so these letters go on top.

parts.note: a rave is an all-night dance party
l is the standard short form of left

explanation.surface: Getting tangled up with a party of the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party on left' reads as politics and the party is the all-night kind. Ravel faces both ways as a word — it can mean to tangle and to untangle — and the clue takes the tangling sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To ravel is to become tangled or knotted, the state loose thread works itself into when nobody is watching.

clue.text: Second vehicle provides wound protection

parts.note: s is the second on a stopwatch
a cab is a taxi, the shortest vehicle on the road

explanation.surface: A back-up car that turns up carrying the first-aid kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second vehicle' looks like one item, the next car in the line, and is two separate instructions. 'Provides' joins the halves and contributes no letters at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A scab is the hard crust that forms over a cut, sealing the wound until the skin underneath has healed.

clue.text: Doorstep lacking its end material

indicators.note: A word lacking its end stops one letter short, so the final letter never gets written.

parts.note: in Britain, to doorstep people is to call at their homes one after another after votes or a quote, and the seven-letter verb for that is the word before the loss

explanation.surface: A doorstep missing the material from its far end.
explanation.walkthrough: Doorstep is a noun on the surface and a verb in the wordplay — what canvassers and reporters do when they turn up at your door unannounced. Only the last letter separates the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Canvas is the heavy woven cloth of tents, sails and artists' stretchers, so 'material' is the plain category word for it.

clue.text: A large French supermarket has no opening outside

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: with no opening, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: Tesco is Britain's largest supermarket chain

explanation.surface: A big French supermarket has yet to open its doors.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesco is a British supermarket chain; 'has no opening' strips its first letter T, leaving ESCO.
explanation.definitionFit: Al fresco means in the open air, as in eating outside.

clue.text: Ruled again to recruit Conservative, being laid back

indicators.note: To recruit somebody is to take them into the ranks, so the letter joins the word from inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: to rule a page is to line it, and doing it over is relining; the word opens after its second letter
c is the letter beside a Conservative name on election night

explanation.surface: A decision handed down a second time so as to sign up a Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid back' is the relaxed idiom on the surface and the literal posture in the answer. 'Ruled' is the pen-and-ruler sense rather than the monarch's.
explanation.definitionFit: To recline is to lean back until you are lying down, so somebody reclined has literally been laid back against the seat.

clue.text: Rocky Bay houses our poor African people

indicators.note: houses means holds inside, so the second reworked piece goes into the first
rocky means unsteady, so the letters of bay are shaken into a new order
poor means in bad shape, so the letters of our are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rugged bay is home to some of our impoverished people from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' makes YBA from BAY, which 'houses' ORU from 'our', made 'poor'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yoruba are a major ethnic group of south-western Nigeria and Benin.
